extracted.intended_audience: communication/media researchers, students, and scholars interested in methods for evaluating news/media content
extracted.subtask_description: Describes and evaluates methodological approaches that compare media content to external (extra-media) benchmarks—statistical indicators, participant observation, and expert opinion—to assess the quality and realism of news coverage. Discusses examples, strengths, and limitations of each approach.

rubrics_metrics.name: Extra-media data (methodological approach)
rubrics_metrics.description: The term “extra-media data” describes a methodological approach to assessing the quality of media content.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Coined by Rosengren (1970) as an alternative to analysing only internal news factors; involves comparing media coverage to external, primarily statistical indicators (e.g., country size, GNP, election outcomes) or other reality indicators to judge whether media emphasis matches 'objective' news value.

rubrics_metrics.name: Statistical-data comparison
rubrics_metrics.description: Evaluate media coverage by comparing the amount/emphasis of coverage to statistical indicators of the underlying issue or event (e.g., country size, GNP, death tolls, number of soldiers, unemployment figures, pollution statistics).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: Rosengren compared parliamentary election coverage to archival country/election data; Funkhouser (1973) compared number of news articles on issues to statistical indicators of salience (found little correlation with statistics but strong correlation with public opinion); Kepplinger (1992) compared ecological coverage with pollution statistics; Adams (1986) compared death tolls of disasters with news emphasis. Use caution: single statistical measures often capture only one aspect of an event.

rubrics_metrics.name: Participant-observation / live-vs-broadcast comparison
rubrics_metrics.description: Assess media representation by comparing impressions of people who experienced an event firsthand with impressions of those who watched broadcast coverage of the same event.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Lang & Lang (1953) and Donsbach et al. (1993) used this method (e.g., parade and campaign speech) and found television often creates different, often stronger or worse, impressions than actual participation — potentially due to the camera's presence or editing choices.

rubrics_metrics.name: Expert-opinion benchmarking
rubrics_metrics.description: Use surveys or assessments of domain experts as an external benchmark and compare that distribution/opinion to the expert views represented or cited in the media.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: Lichter et al. (1986) surveyed nuclear-energy experts and compared to media-cited experts; Snyderman & Rothman (1988) surveyed intelligence experts and compared to media coverage of the IQ controversy. Studies found media can misrepresent the distribution of expert opinion. Beware that experts themselves may be biased or unrepresentative.

rubrics_metrics.name: Indicator-selection validity (indicators may capture only part of the issue)
rubrics_metrics.description: Concrete indicators used for comparison often represent only a certain aspect of the issue or event they are supposed to indicate (e.g., using number of American GIs as indicator for Vietnam War salience).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Researchers must recognize that a chosen statistic may not fully represent the ‘objective’ importance or salience of an issue; multiple indicators or nuanced interpretation may be needed to avoid misleading conclusions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Bias in indicators and expert benchmarks
rubrics_metrics.description: Extra-media indicators and expert measures may themselves be biased and thus may not serve as neutral benchmarks.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The page notes that experts or statistical sources can carry biases (example: expert opinions may be skewed); researchers should assess the reliability and representativeness of external benchmarks before using them to judge media accuracy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Applicability limitation: absence of extra-media data
rubrics_metrics.description: There are many areas of media coverage where no suitable extra-media data exist to assess media content.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When no external data are available, extra-media comparison cannot be applied; alternative evaluative approaches (e.g., discourse analysis, audience studies) may be necessary.

rubrics_metrics.name: Epistemological critique: no universal benchmark for media reality construction
rubrics_metrics.description: Schulz (1976) argued that each system constructs reality by its own criteria and therefore there may be no universal benchmark for evaluating media content.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This critique implies that comparing media to external 'objective' measures is contested: different systems' criteria for what counts as reality will differ from news factors, so claims of objective benchmarking should be made cautiously.

rubrics_metrics.name: Overall assessment: conditional strength of extra-media comparisons
rubrics_metrics.description: If one assumes that some scientific measure of the quality of reality representation in the media is important, comparison of media content with extra-media data is probably the strongest tool.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Despite the limitations and critiques listed, the page concludes that extra-media comparisons remain a powerful method when appropriate indicators are available and when their limitations are acknowledged and addressed.
